text.p: Hundreds of scholars lashed out at the ruling Nationalist Party on Friday, saying it was perverting Taiwan's new-found democracy by proposing constitutional reforms to create an unchecked "super-president".

"The Nationalist Party's constitutional amendments (are) to create an emperor, not a democratic government," some 400 scholars said in a joint statement attacking President Lee Teng-hui's governing party.

"It reminds us of Yuan Shih-kai, who tried to use political assembly to change the constitution in order to create a super president system without checks and balances," they said, warning of a new historical tragedy.

Yuan, a military strongman nearly a century ago, was named the first president of the new Chinese republic that overthrew the Qing dynasty in 1911 -- only to annul the new constitution and proclaim himself emperor in 1915.

The scholars took their attack public after the Nationalist Party spurned their call to abandon a slate of constitutional amendments widely seen as boosting the president's power at the expense of the fully elected Legislative Yuan, or parliament.
The National Assembly, an elective body whose sole function is to revise the constitution and whose membership is mostly Nationalist, is expected to adopt the resolutions by June 30.
Under the proposals, the president no longer would need parliament's consent to appoint the cabinet head or premier and would have power to dissolve parliament when he deems necessary.
They would make explicit the president's powers to dictate policy towards defence, foreign affairs, China and other national security issues, which now are not defined in the constitution.

Parliament can currently undermine a premier with a no-confidence vote of two-thirds of its members, but has no power to unseat the president or vice president, who since March 1996 have been elected through popular vote.

The amendments would give parliament power to recall a president, but set a very high standard -- requiring a three-fifths vote of the full membership to impeach the chief executive and a two-thirds vote to sack him.
The president would be able to implement unilaterally bills that have been stalled in parliament for more than a year.
Taiwan's constitutional and legal scholars say that goes too far, threatening the island's hard-won democracy.
"The proposed amendments seriously distort democratic principles, creating an all-powerful president who could easily play the role of an emperor," said law professor Hu Fu.
Another prominent politics professor, Chang Lin-chen, said the amendments insulated the president from political scrutiny.
"Worst of all, the president need not face the checks and balances of parliament, and the premier is in effect a chief of staff to the president," Chang said.

Even before the reform drive, President Lee and his vice president, Lien Chan, have come under intense political fire and even a high court challenge because Lee gave Lien the additional job of premier.
